idiom_name: extension table keyed by an id (or a GLib-style dataset) + function-pointer interface struct
implementation_notes: C has no classes, methods or per-object attribute storage, so the whole structure is hand-written: an extension table (array or hash map of {key, void *}) plus a lookup function get_extension(subject, key) that returns NULL when the capability is absent. If the struct is yours, the table lives inside it; if it is opaque (a third-party or library type), the table is keyed by the object's address - which is exactly what GLib datasets formalise: 'Since you cannot modify the structure, you use its location in memory as the key into a dataset, where you can associate any number of data elements with it'. The behaviour half degrades to a struct of function pointers stored as the extension payload (the moral equivalent of AbstractExtension), which the client casts to the interface it asked for.
pitfalls: A side table keyed by the object's address is only valid while that object exists: you must hook destruction or finalisation to remove the entry, otherwise a recycled address inherits a stale extension and the lookup returns a valid-looking pointer of the wrong type.

String keys are interned by libraries such as GLib (g_quark_from_string) and the interned key lives forever, so generating keys dynamically leaks unbounded quarks; use a unique address per extension (a static symbol or an enum id) instead of ad-hoc strings.

Nothing in the C type system distinguishes one extension payload from another: the client's cast to the interface struct is unchecked, so a wrong or stale key is undefined behaviour rather than a failed lookup.

Extension tables stored inside the struct change the object's layout - if the type is part of a published ABI, that breaks binary compatibility, which is precisely the case the pattern is meant to leave untouched.
